proofs.proof_tex:
Fix \(P\in\mathcal M\), \(x\in\mathcal X\), and \((s,t)\in\mathbb R^2\).  Using \(S_j=A+U_j\), first condition on \((A,X,Y)\).  Error--latent independence and coordinate independence give
\[
\begin{aligned}
F_x(s,t)
&=E_P\!\left[\mathbf 1\{X=x\}e^{i(s+t)A}
 E_P(e^{isU_1})E_P(e^{itU_2})\right]\\
&=p_x\varphi_{f,x}(s+t)\varphi_1(s)\varphi_2(t).
\end{aligned}
\]
The same conditioning, now retaining the bounded mark \(Y\), gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
G_x(s,t)
&=E_P\!\left[\mathbf 1\{X=x\}Y e^{i(s+t)A}\right]
  \varphi_1(s)\varphi_2(t)\\
&=p_x\left\{\int_{\mathcal A}e^{i(s+t)a}m_x(a)f_x(a)\,da\right\}
  \varphi_1(s)\varphi_2(t)\\
&=p_x\varphi_{q,x}(s+t)\varphi_1(s)\varphi_2(t).
\end{aligned}
\]
All conditional integrals exist because consistency and bounded potential outcomes imply \(|Y|\le B_Y\) almost surely.  Finally, \(|e^{iv}-1|\le|v|\), Cauchy--Schwarz, and the second-moment assumption imply, for \(|u|\le\nu_*\),
\[
 |\varphi_j(u)|\ge1-E_P|e^{iuU_j}-1|
 \ge1-|u|E_P|U_j|
 \ge1-|u|\sqrt{M_e}\ge\frac12.
\]
This proves both factorizations and the protected-frequency bound.

The observed law gives \(p_x=P_{\mathrm{obs}}(X=x)\).  Fix \(x\).  Choose
\[
 \rho=\min\{\nu_*/4,(8B_A)^{-1}\}>0.
\]
For \(|s|,|t|\le2\rho\), compact dose support and \(|e^{iv}-1|\le|v|\) imply
\[
 |\varphi_{f,x}(s+t)|\ge1-B_A|s+t|\ge\frac12.
\]
Together with stratum positivity and the protected-frequency bound, this shows that \(F_x\) has no zero on that square.

Differentiate the factorization with respect to \(t\) at \((s,0)\).  The derivative exists because \(A\) is bounded and \(E|U_2|<\infty\).  Since \(\varphi_2'(0)=iE_PU_2=0\),
\[
 \frac{\partial_tF_x(s,0)}{F_x(s,0)}
 =\frac{\varphi_{f,x}'(s)}{\varphi_{f,x}(s)},\qquad |s|\le2\rho. \tag{18}
\]
The right side solves the scalar differential equation with initial value \(\varphi_{f,x}(0)=1\); hence the observed law identifies
\[
 \varphi_{f,x}(s)=\exp\left\{\int_0^s
 \frac{\partial_tF_x(u,0)}{F_x(u,0)}\,du\right\},
 \qquad |s|\le2\rho. \tag{19}
\]
Because \(f_x\) is supported on \(\mathcal A\), its transform is entire.  Two entire functions agreeing on the real interval in (19) agree everywhere by the power-series identity argument: their difference has all derivatives zero at any interior accumulation point.  Thus \(\varphi_{f,x}\), and by Fourier uniqueness \(f_x\) almost everywhere, is identified.  Since \(\beta>1/2\), the Fourier Cauchy--Schwarz bound makes every \(H^\beta\) function continuous, so the continuous version of \(f_x\) is identified pointwise.

On the same interval the common nuisance factor cancels:
\[
 \frac{G_x(s,0)}{F_x(s,0)}
 =\frac{\varphi_{q,x}(s)}{\varphi_{f,x}(s)}. \tag{20}
\]
Equations (19)--(20) identify \(\varphi_{q,x}\) locally.  The bounded outcome and compact dose support make \(q_x\) integrable and supported on \(\mathcal A\), so its transform is entire.  The same identity and Fourier-uniqueness arguments identify \(q_x\), and its \(H^\beta\) membership again yields its pointwise continuous version.

It remains to connect this observed-law functional to the causal target.  Consistency and conditional unconfoundedness imply, at dose values for which the conditional regression is defined,
\[
 E_P\{Y(a)\mid X=x\}=E_P(Y\mid A=a,X=x)=m_x(a)=\frac{q_x(a)}{f_x(a)}. \tag{21}
\]
Division is valid on \(I\) because dose overlap gives \(f_x(a)\ge\kappa>0\).  The quotient in (21) is continuous because \(f_x,q_x\in H^\beta\) and \(\beta>1/2\); the left side has the continuous version required by causal-mean continuity.  Equality almost everywhere therefore extends to every \(a\in I\).  Averaging (21) over the finite strata proves
\[
 \mu(a)=\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}p_x\frac{q_x(a)}{f_x(a)},\qquad a\in I,
\]
and every quantity on the right has already been identified from \(P_{\mathrm{obs}}\).

For the true law \(P\), each empirical channel is an average of independent complex variables.  At every \((s,t)\),
\[
 E|\widehat F_{x,n}(s,t)-F_x(s,t)|^2
 =\frac1n\operatorname{Var}\{\mathbf 1(X=x)e^{i(sS_1+tS_2)}\}
 \le\frac{p_x}{n}.
\]
Consistency and bounded potential outcomes give \(|Y|\le B_Y\) almost surely, and hence
\[
 B_Y^{-2}E|\widehat G_{x,n}(s,t)-G_x(s,t)|^2\le\frac{p_x}{n}.
\]
Likewise, \(E|\widehat p_x-p_x|^2\le p_x/n\).  Tonelli's theorem is applicable because every integrand is nonnegative.  Since \(|\mathcal C_*|=4\nu_*^2\) and \(\sum_xp_x=1\), summing and integrating gives the uniform bound
\[
 \sup_{P\in\mathcal M}E_{P_{\mathrm{obs}}^{\otimes n}}\mathscr D_n(P)
 \le\frac{8\nu_*^2+1}{n}. \tag{22}
\]
Markov's inequality and the definition of \(\epsilon_n\) now yield
\[
 \sup_{P\in\mathcal M}P_{\mathrm{obs}}^{\otimes n}
 \{\mathscr D_n(P)>\epsilon_n^2\}
 \le\frac{8\nu_*^2+1}{C_\alpha^2\log(en/\alpha)}.
\]
Choose a fixed \(C_\alpha>0\).  The last expression is at most \(\alpha\) for all sufficiently large \(n\), proving the proposition.  The second-moment condition is used to make \(\nu_*\) a fixed positive radius; no frequency grid is invoked.

We prove the claim by making explicit the compactness and enclosure facts used by the stated algorithm.  First, for \(h\) supported on \(\mathcal A\) with \(\|h\|_{H^\beta}\le R\), Fourier inversion and Cauchy--Schwarz give
\[
 \|h\|_\infty\le C R,
 \qquad
 |h(a)-h(a')|\le C R|a-a'|^{\beta-1/2\wedge1}.
\]
More generally, truncating the Fourier integral at frequency \(T\) gives a uniform remainder at most \(CRT^{1/2-\beta}\).  Thus the density and marked-density balls, restricted to \(I\), are totally bounded in the uniform norm.  A Fourier mesh followed by outward interval rounding gives, at accuracy \(u\), at most
\[
 \exp\{C u^{-1/(\beta-1/2)}\log(C/u)\} \tag{30}
\]
boxes.  This count follows by taking \(T\asymp u^{-1/(\beta-1/2)}\), using mesh width of order \(u/T\), and quantizing each bounded Fourier coefficient outward.

Second, Markov's inequality applied to the error second moments gives
\[
 Q(|U_j|>T)\le M_e/T^2. \tag{31}
\]
On \([-T,T]\), positive quadrature exact for monomials through order \(2K_n\) is obtained directly as follows.  The moment vector lies in the convex hull of the moment curve \((1,u,\ldots,u^{2K_n})\).  If a convex representation has more than \(2K_n+2\) support points, affine dependence permits one weight to be reduced to zero without changing the vector; iteration leaves at most \(2K_n+2\) positive atoms.  Taylor's formula encloses the exponential remainder, while (31) encloses the two tails.  Subdivision of atom locations, weights, tails, and remainder values therefore gives finite outward boxes for both error transforms.  Products and integrals are enclosed by the natural complex interval operations.  The same argument applies simultaneously to every stratum and to the probability and marked channels.

The algorithm retains a box only with its outward constraint certificate and subdivides until the radius of every constraint and objective interval is at most \(\zeta_n\).  Total boundedness of the preceding parameter sets implies that a finite subdivision attains this tolerance.  Every exact candidate \(Q\in\Theta_{n,\alpha}\) belongs to one of the boxes because Taylor, tail, quadrature, and rounding intervals were all taken outward.  Hence
\[
 \Theta_{n,\alpha}\subseteq
 \bigcup_{b\in\mathscr B_{n,\alpha}}\operatorname{Dec}_n(b)
 =\Theta^{\mathrm{cert}}_{n,\alpha}\subseteq\mathcal M. \tag{32}
\]
The last inclusion holds because the decoder admits only laws in \(\mathcal M\).  Interval evaluation preserves inclusion under addition, multiplication, and division whenever the denominator interval is bounded away from zero.  Here that division is valid because it is intersected with \([\kappa,\infty)\).  Thus
\[
 \{\mu_Q(a):Q\in\operatorname{Dec}_n(b)\}\subseteq J_{b,n}(a). \tag{33}
\]

For a retained box meeting the exact profile, every value of its objective interval differs by at most \(C\zeta_n\) from the objective of a represented exact-profile law.  Boxes certified disjoint from the constraint set are discarded.  Applying this fact to the boxes containing minimizers and maximizers, and using compactness to pass to a minimizing or maximizing subsequence, gives uniformly in \(a\in I\)
\[
 0\le\inf_{Q\in\Theta_{n,\alpha}}\mu_Q(a)-\underline m_n^{\mathrm{cert}}(a)
 \le C\zeta_n,
\]
\[
 0\le\overline m_n^{\mathrm{cert}}(a)-\sup_{Q\in\Theta_{n,\alpha}}\mu_Q(a)
 \le C\zeta_n. \tag{34}
\]
These statements are conditional only on nonemptiness of the exact profile, as required.

It remains to check the announced finite size.  For sufficiently large \(n\), the definition of \(K_n\) implies
\[
 \log(en)\asymp K_n\log K_n,
 \qquad
 \zeta_n\asymp K_n^{-\beta-1/2}(\log K_n)^{-1}. \tag{35}
\]
Because \(\beta>3/2\),
\[
 \zeta_n^{-1/(\beta-1/2)}\log(C/\zeta_n)
 \le C K_n^2\log(K_n/\zeta_n). \tag{36}
\]
The coefficient, positive-quadrature, tail, and remainder descriptions have at most \(CK_n^2\) scalar coordinates; quantizing each at outward resolution proportional to \(\zeta_n/K_n^2\), and combining (30) and (36), proves
\[
 |\mathscr B_{n,\alpha}|\le
 \exp\{CK_n^2\log(K_n/\zeta_n)\}.
\]
Finally, \(\zeta_n/r_n=1/\log(en)\to0\), so (34) also gives \(C\zeta_n=o(r_n)\).  This proves termination, coverage, endpoint accuracy, and the certificate-count bound.

Let \(E_P=\{\mathscr D_n(P)\le\epsilon_n^2\}\).  The concentration proposition gives
\[
 \inf_{P\in\mathcal M}P_{\mathrm{obs}}^{\otimes n}(E_P)\ge1-\alpha. \tag{37}
\]
On \(E_P\), the true law belongs to \(\Theta_{n,\alpha}\), hence to \(\Theta^{\mathrm{cert}}_{n,\alpha}\) by the finite-profile theorem.  Its ADRF lies in every outward endpoint enclosure relevant to its decoded box.  Since \(|\mu_P(a)|\le B_Y\), clipping at \([-B_Y,B_Y]\) cannot remove the true value.  Therefore, on \(E_P\),
\[
 L_n(a)\le\mu_P(a)\le U_n(a)\quad\text{for every }a\in I. \tag{38}
\]
Equations (37)--(38), joint measurability of the finite interval operations, and the construction \(L_n\le U_n\) prove \((L_n,U_n)\in\mathfrak B_{n,\alpha}\).

We next bound width on every sample, not merely on \(E_P\).  The square root of \(\mathscr D_n\) is a Hilbert-product norm.  Thus, for any \(Q,R\in\Theta_{n,\alpha}\), the triangle inequality gives
\[
 d(Q,R)\le \mathscr D_n(Q)^{1/2}+\mathscr D_n(R)^{1/2}le2\epsilon_n. \tag{39}
\]
The paired protected inverse theorem applied to (39) yields
\[
 \sup_{Q,R\in\Theta_{n,\alpha}}\|\mu_Q-\mu_R\|_{L^\infty(I)}
 \le C\left\{\frac{\log\log(1/\epsilon_n)}{\log(1/\epsilon_n)}\right\}^{\beta-1/2}
 \le Cr_n, \tag{40}
\]
where the last comparison follows from \(\epsilon_n\asymp\sqrt{\log n/n}\) and \(K_n\asymp\log n/\log\log n\).  The certified endpoint theorem changes each exact endpoint by at most \(C\zeta_n=o(r_n)\).  Therefore (40) and the definition of the clipped band imply \(W_n\le Cr_n\) whenever the profile is nonempty; if it is empty, \(W_n=0\).  This deterministic bound gives
\[
 \sup_{P\in\mathcal M}E_{P_{\mathrm{obs}}^{\otimes n}}W_n\le Cr_n.
\]
The same class \(\mathcal M\) is used in (37)--(40), so the conclusion is uniform over the stated model.

Apply the fixed-kernel Bernoulli packet lemma with
\[
 k_n=\left\lceil\frac{\log(en)}{\log\log(e^e n)}\right\rceil
\]
and set \(P_{j,n}=P_{j,k_n}\).  The construction in that lemma verifies directly that both laws belong to \(\mathcal M\), that their stratum masses, density \(f^\circ\), and two nonidentical asymmetric error laws are fixed and common, and that their conditional marks are Bernoulli.  Since \(c_K>0\) is fixed,
\[
 k_n\asymp K_n,
 \qquad
 \|\mu_{1,n}-\mu_{0,n}\|_{L^\infty(I)}
 \ge c k_n^{1/2-\beta}\ge c r_n. \tag{41}
\]

For product measures the chi-square identity is
\[
 1+\chi^2(P_{1,n,\mathrm{obs}}^{\otimes n},P_{0,n,\mathrm{obs}}^{\otimes n})
 =\{1+\chi^2(P_{1,n,\mathrm{obs}},P_{0,n,\mathrm{obs}})\}^n. \tag{42}
\]
The packet bound and \(m!\ge(m/e)^m\) show
\[
 n\chi^2(P_{1,n,\mathrm{obs}},P_{0,n,\mathrm{obs}})
 \le Cn\frac{C_0^{4k_n}}{\{(2k_n-4)!\}^2}\longrightarrow0. \tag{43}
\]
Indeed, the logarithm of the right side is at most \(\log n-4k_n\log k_n+O(k_n)\), which tends to \(-\infty\).  Equations (42)--(43) imply that the product chi-square divergence tends to zero.  Finally,
\[
 \|P_{1,n,\mathrm{obs}}^{\otimes n}-P_{0,n,\mathrm{obs}}^{\otimes n}\|_{\mathrm{TV}}
 \le\left\{\frac12\chi^2(P_{1,n,\mathrm{obs}}^{\otimes n},P_{0,n,\mathrm{obs}}^{\otimes n})\right\}^{1/2}\longrightarrow0.
\]
It is consequently at most the prescribed \(\eta>0\) for all sufficiently large \(n\).  Together with (41), this proves the theorem.

The upper bound follows immediately because the certified band is one admissible element of \(\mathfrak B_{n,\alpha}\):
\[
 \mathfrak R_n
 \le\sup_{P\in\mathcal M}E_{P_{\mathrm{obs}}^{\otimes n}}W_n
 \le Cr_n. \tag{44}
\]
For the lower bound, take any \((L_n,U_n)\in\mathfrak B_{n,\alpha}\) and the two laws from the fixed-nuisance marked-pair theorem.  Let
\[
 A_j=\{L_n(a)\le\mu_{j,n}(a)\le U_n(a)\text{ for every }a\in I\},
 \qquad j=0,1.
\]
Honesty gives \(P_{j,n,\mathrm{obs}}^{\otimes n}(A_j)\ge1-\alpha\).  The total-variation bound gives
\[
 P_{0,n,\mathrm{obs}}^{\otimes n}(A_1)
 \ge P_{1,n,\mathrm{obs}}^{\otimes n}(A_1)-\eta
 \ge1-\alpha-\eta.
\]
Consequently,
\[
 P_{0,n,\mathrm{obs}}^{\otimes n}(A_0\cap A_1)
 \ge1-2\alpha-\eta>0. \tag{45}
\]
On \(A_0\cap A_1\), both curves lie in the band at every dose, and hence
\[
 W_n\ge\|\mu_{1,n}-\mu_{0,n}\|_{L^\infty(I)}\ge cr_n.
\]
Taking expectations and using (45) gives
\[
 \sup_{P\in\mathcal M}E_{P_{\mathrm{obs}}^{\otimes n}}W_n
 \ge c(1-2\alpha-\eta)r_n.
\]
This holds for every honest band.  Taking the infimum proves the lower bound in \(\mathfrak R_n\).  Finally, the definitions of \(K_n\) and \(r_n\), with fixed \(c_K>0\), give
\[
 r_n\asymp\left\{\frac{\log\log n}{\log n}\right\}^{\beta-1/2},
\]
which proves the equivalent display.

On the stated submodel, \(U_1=U_2=0\) almost surely, so \(\varphi_1(s)=\varphi_2(t)=1\) for every \(s,t\).  Substitution into the paired-channel factorization gives
\[
 F_x(s,t)=p_x\varphi_{f,x}(s+t),
 \qquad
 G_x(s,t)=p_x\varphi_{q,x}(s+t).
\]
The identification theorem is unchanged and yields, using \(q_x=m_xf_x\) and overlap on \(I\),
\[
 \mu(a)=\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}p_x\frac{q_x(a)}{f_x(a)}
 =\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}p_xE_P[Y\mid A=a,X=x].
\]
Consistency, conditional unconfoundedness, and causal-mean continuity identify the last display with \(E_PY(a)\) at every \(a\in I\), exactly as in equation (21).  Thus the blind-replicate functional reduces to the ordinary continuous-treatment g-formula.

theorem.statement:
There are constants \(c,C>0\), depending only on the fixed constants of \(\mathcal M\), such that, for every sufficiently small \(\delta>0\), all \(P,Q\in\mathcal M\) satisfying
\[
 \sum_{x\in\mathcal X}\left\{\int_{\mathcal C_*}\left(
 |F_{x,P}-F_{x,Q}|^2+B_Y^{-2}|G_{x,P}-G_{x,Q}|^2\right)\,ds\,dt
 +|p_{x,P}-p_{x,Q}|^2\right\}\le\delta^2
\]
satisfy
\[
 \|\mu_P-\mu_Q\|_{L^\infty(I)}
 \le C\left\{\frac{\log\log(1/\delta)}{\log(1/\delta)}\right\}^{\beta-1/2}.
\]
Conversely, for every sufficiently small \(\delta\), there are two members of a submodel with fixed \(p_x\), fixed \(f_x=f^\circ\), fixed nonidentical asymmetric error laws, and conditionally Bernoulli outcomes, whose paired-channel discrepancy is at most \(\delta^2\) while their ADRFs are separated by at least
\[
 c\left\{\frac{\log\log(1/\delta)}{\log(1/\delta)}\right\}^{\beta-1/2}.
\]
Thus the exponent \(\beta-1/2\) is unimprovable on that fixed-nuisance marked submodel.
theorem.proof_tex:
Write \(d(P,Q)\) for the square root of the discrepancy in the question and assume \(d(P,Q)\le\delta\).  Put
\[
 \rho=\min\{\nu_*/4,(8B_A)^{-1}\}.
\]
The square \([-2\rho,2\rho]^2\) lies in \(\mathcal C_*\).  For either law, the bounds \(|\varphi_j(u)|\ge1/2\), \(|\varphi_{f,x}(v)|\ge1-B_A|v|\ge1/2\), and \(p_x\ge p_{\min}\) imply
\[
 |F_x(s,t)|\ge p_{\min}/8,
 \qquad |s|,|t|\le2\rho. \tag{23}
\]

We first convert integrated channel distance to uniform local distance.  Each probability channel has uniformly bounded first derivatives because
\[
 E|S_j|\le B_A+\sqrt{M_e},
\]
and each marked channel has the same derivative bound multiplied by \(B_Y\).  If a Lipschitz function \(H\) on the outer square has maximum modulus \(M\) on the inner square, integration over a disk of radius proportional to \(M\) around a maximizer gives
\[
 M\le C\|H\|_{L^2([-2\rho,2\rho]^2)}^{1/2}
\]
when the latter norm is sufficiently small.  Applying this inequality to the channel differences gives
\[
 \max_x\left(\|F_{x,P}-F_{x,Q}\|_{\infty,[-\rho,\rho]^2}
 +B_Y^{-1}\|G_{x,P}-G_{x,Q}\|_{\infty,[-\rho,\rho]^2}\right)
 \le C\delta^{1/2}. \tag{24}
\]
The second \(t\)-derivatives of the probability channels are uniformly bounded, since
\[
 E S_2^2\le2(B_A^2+M_e).
\]
For a twice differentiable function \(h\) on \([-\rho,\rho]\), Taylor's formula at steps \(v\) and \(-v\), optimized at \(v\asymp\|h\|_\infty^{1/2}\), gives
\[
 |h'(0)|\le C\{\|h\|_\infty^{1/2}+\|h\|_\infty\}.
\]
Use this with \(h(t)=F_{x,P}(s,t)-F_{x,Q}(s,t)\) and (24), uniformly for \(|s|\le\rho\), to obtain
\[
 \sup_{|s|\le\rho}|\partial_tF_{x,P}(s,0)-\partial_tF_{x,Q}(s,0)|
 \le C\delta^{1/4}. \tag{25}
\]

The centered-second-error normalization and factorization give
\[
 \frac{\partial_tF_{x,P}(s,0)}{F_{x,P}(s,0)}
 =\frac{\varphi_{f,x,P}'(s)}{\varphi_{f,x,P}(s)},
\]
and the analogous identity under \(Q\).  Equations (23)--(25), followed by integration from zero to \(s\), therefore show
\[
 \sup_{|s|\le\rho}|\varphi_{f,x,P}(s)-\varphi_{f,x,Q}(s)|
 \le C\delta^{1/4}. \tag{26}
\]
Moreover, cancellation of the common nuisance factor within each law gives
\[
 \frac{G_{x,P}(s,0)}{F_{x,P}(s,0)}
 =\frac{\varphi_{q,x,P}(s)}{\varphi_{f,x,P}(s)}.
\]
Using (23), (24), (26), and \(|\varphi_{q,x}|le B_Y\) yields
\[
 \sup_{|s|\le\rho}|\varphi_{q,x,P}(s)-\varphi_{q,x,Q}(s)|
 \le C\delta^{1/4}. \tag{27}
\]

Apply the continuous analytic Sobolev modulus lemma to \(f_{x,P}-f_{x,Q}\) and \(q_{x,P}-q_{x,Q}\).  Their supports lie in \(\mathcal A\), their Sobolev norms are bounded by \(2R_f\) and \(2R_q\), and their \(L^1\) norms are bounded by \(2\) and \(2B_Y\), respectively.  Equations (26)--(27) consequently give, with
\[
 \omega(\delta)=\left\{\frac{\log\log(1/\delta)}{\log(1/\delta)}\right\}^{\beta-1/2},
\]
the bounds
\[
 \max_x\left(\|f_{x,P}-f_{x,Q}\|_\infty+
 \|q_{x,P}-q_{x,Q}\|_\infty\right)\le C\omega(\delta). \tag{28}
\]
Also the discrepancy directly gives \(\max_x|p_{x,P}-p_{x,Q}|\le\delta\).  Since \(f_{x,P},f_{x,Q}\ge\kappa\) on \(I\) and \(|q_{x,Q}|\le B_Yf_{x,Q}\),
\[
 \left|\frac{q_{x,P}}{f_{x,P}}-\frac{q_{x,Q}}{f_{x,Q}}\right|
 \le\kappa^{-1}|q_{x,P}-q_{x,Q}|+B_Y\kappa^{-1}|f_{x,P}-f_{x,Q}|. \tag{29}
\]
Combining (28)--(29), the finite sum in the identifying functional, and the mass difference proves the upper modulus.

For the converse, use the fixed-kernel Bernoulli packet lemma with
\[
 k(\delta)=\left\lceil c_0\frac{\log(1/\delta)}{\log\log(1/\delta)}\right\rceil
\]
and choose the fixed \(c_0\) large enough.  The factorial inequality \(m!\ge(m/e)^m\) implies
\[
 C\frac{C_0^{4k(\delta)}}{\{(2k(\delta)-4)!\}^2}\le c\delta^2
\]
for all sufficiently small \(\delta\).  The probability channels are identical.  For the marked channels, the difference of the expectation of a complex random variable bounded by one is at most twice total variation, and \(2\operatorname{TV}^2\le\chi^2\).  Since \(\mathcal C_*\) has finite volume, the paired-channel discrepancy is therefore at most \(\delta^2\), after increasing \(c_0\) once.  The separation supplied by that lemma is
\[
 ck(\delta)^{1/2-\beta}\ge c\omega(\delta).
\]
All unmarked nuisances are fixed across this pair, so this proves the stated sharpness on the asserted submodel.

added_lemmas.statement:
Let \(\widehat h(t)=\int_{\mathcal A}e^{ita}h(a)\,da\).  For every fixed \(\rho>0\) there are constants \(c,C,C_0>0\), depending only on \(B_A,\beta,\rho\), such that every \(h\in H^\beta(\mathbb R)\) supported in \(\mathcal A\), with \(\|h\|_{H^\beta}\le R\), \(\|h\|_1\le M\), and \(\|\widehat h\|_{L^2[-\rho,\rho]}\le\varepsilon\), satisfies, for every integer \(k\ge1\),
\[
 \|h\|_\infty\le C\left[Rk^{1/2-\beta}+k(C_0k)^k\varepsilon+Mk e^{-ck}\right].
\]
Consequently, for all sufficiently small \(\varepsilon\),
\[
 \|h\|_\infty\le C(R+M)\left\{\frac{\log\log(1/\varepsilon)}{\log(1/\varepsilon)}\right\}^{\beta-1/2}.
\]
added_lemmas.proof_tex:
Put \(H(z)=\int_{-B_A}^{B_A}e^{iza}h(a)\,da\).  Absolute convergence and differentiation under the integral give
\[
 H^{(j)}(z)=\int_{-B_A}^{B_A}(ia)^j e^{iza}h(a)\,da,
 \qquad |H^{(j)}(0)|\le M B_A^j .
\]
Let \(T_k(z)=\sum_{j=0}^kH^{(j)}(0)z^j/j!\).  Taylor's formula, applied inside the integral, yields the two bounds
\[
 |H(t)-T_k(t)|\le M\frac{(B_A|t|)^{k+1}}{(k+1)!},
 \qquad t\in\mathbb R. \tag{1}
\]
We next record the elementary polynomial extrapolation inequality
\[
 sup_{|t|\le T}|p(t)|
 \le C\rho^{-1/2}\left(\frac{C(1+T)}{\rho}\right)^k
 \|p\|_{L^2[-\rho,\rho]},\qquad T\ge\rho, \tag{2}
\]
for every polynomial \(p\) of degree at most \(k\).  To verify (2), rescale to \([-1,1]\), expand \(p\) in the orthonormal Legendre basis, use Cauchy--Schwarz for its coefficients, and use the explicit three-term recursion to obtain \(|P_j(x)|\le(2|x|+1)^j\) for \(|x|\ge1\).  Summing the resulting geometric bound for \(0\le j\le k\) proves (2), including its displayed constants.

Apply (2) to \(T_k\).  On \([-\rho,\rho]\), (1) and the hypothesis give
\[
 \|T_k\|_2\le\varepsilon+(2\rho)^{1/2}M\frac{(B_A\rho)^{k+1}}{(k+1)!}. \tag{3}
\]
Choose a fixed \(a_0>0\), depending only on \(B_A\) and \(\rho\), small enough that \(T=a_0k\) makes both
\[
 \left\{C(1+T)/\rho\right\}^k\frac{(B_A\rho)^{k+1}}{(k+1)!}
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 \frac{(B_AT)^{k+1}}{(k+1)!}
\]
at most \(Ce^{-ck}\).  This follows directly from \((k+1)!\ge((k+1)/e)^{k+1}\), which itself follows by integrating \(\log x\) from \(1\) to \(k+1\).  Equations (1)--(3) therefore imply
\[
 sup_{|t|\le T}|H(t)|\le (C_0k)^k\varepsilon+CMe^{-ck}. \tag{4}
\]
Because \(\beta>1/2\), Fourier inversion is absolutely convergent.  Cauchy--Schwarz and the definition of the Sobolev norm give
\[
 \int_{|t|>T}|H(t)|\,dt
 \le \left\{\int_{|t|>T}(1+t^2)^{-\beta}\,dt\right\}^{1/2}\|h\|_{H^\beta}
 \le CR T^{1/2-\beta}. \tag{5}
\]
Splitting the inversion integral at \(T=a_0k\), and applying (4) and (5), proves the first assertion.

Finally let \(L=\log(1/\varepsilon)\) and choose
\[
 k=\left\lfloor c_1\frac{L}{\log(e+L)}\right\rfloor
\]
with \(c_1>0\) sufficiently small.  Then \(k(C_0k)^k\varepsilon\le Ck^{1/2-\beta}\) and \(ke^{-ck}\le Ck^{1/2-\beta}\) for all sufficiently large \(L\).  Since \(k\asymp L/\log L\), substitution into the first assertion proves the claimed logarithmic modulus.

added_lemmas.statement:
There are fixed, nonidentical, asymmetric error densities \(g_1,g_2\), constants \(c,C,C_0>0\), and, for every sufficiently large integer \(k\), two laws \(P_{0,k},P_{1,k}\in\mathcal M\) with common stratum masses, common latent density \(f_x=f^\circ\), and common error densities \(g_1,g_2\), such that the second error is centered, both error second moments are at most \(M_e\), and the outcomes are conditionally Bernoulli.  Moreover,
\[
 \|\mu_{1,k}-\mu_{0,k}\|_{L^\infty(I)}\ge ck^{1/2-\beta}
\]
and
\[
 \chi^2(P_{1,k,\mathrm{obs}},P_{0,k,\mathrm{obs}})
 \le C\frac{C_0^{4k}}{\{(2k-4)!\}^2}.
\]
The probability channels and the complete unmarked observed laws are identical under the two laws.
added_lemmas.proof_tex:
Choose a closed nondegenerate interval \(J\subset\operatorname{int}(I)\).  We first construct a moment-annihilating packet on \(J\).  After an affine change of variable from \(J\) to \([-1,1]\), fix an integer \(r>\beta+4\), put \(w(z)=(1-z^2)^r\), and let \(\{\pi_j:j\ge0\}\) be the orthonormal polynomial sequence in \(L^2(w(z)\,dz)\).  Define
\[
 K_k(z,0)=\sum_{j=2k}^{4k}\pi_j(0)\pi_j(z),
 \qquad
 \widetilde h_k(a)=w(z(a))K_k(z(a),0)\mathbf 1\{a\in J\}.
\]
Orthogonality gives, for \(0\le \ell<2k\),
\[
 \int_J a^\ell\widetilde h_k(a)\,da=0. \tag{6}
\]
For completeness, the needed size estimates follow from the Rodrigues formula for the Jacobi polynomials with parameters \((r,r)\).  Expanding the derivative in that formula, integrating the resulting beta integrals, and bounding the factorial ratios above and below by their adjacent products gives
\[
 c k\le K_k(0,0)\le Ck,
 \quad \|\widetilde h_k\|_2\le Ck^{1/2},
 \quad \|\widetilde h_k\|_{H^m}\le C_m k^{m+1/2} \tag{7}
\]
for every fixed integer \(m\le r-1\).  The endpoint zero of order \(r\) makes the zero extension belong to \(H^m(\mathbb R)\).  If \(m>\beta\), Holder's inequality in the Fourier definition of the Sobolev norms interpolates the last two bounds in (7) and gives
\[
 \|\widetilde h_k\|_{H^\beta}\le Ck^{\beta+1/2}. \tag{8}
\]
Thus, after multiplication by one fixed sufficiently small constant,
\[
 h_k=k^{-\beta-1/2}\widetilde h_k
\]
satisfies
\[
 \|h_k\|_{H^\beta}\le1,
 \quad \|h_k\|_1\le Ck^{-\beta},
 \quad \|h_k\|_\infty\le Ck^{1/2-\beta},
 \quad |h_k(a_0)|\ge ck^{1/2-\beta} \tag{9}
\]
at the point \(a_0\in J\) corresponding to \(z=0\).  Notice that (6) is unchanged by this scaling.

We next give explicit fixed error laws.  Let
\[
 \psi(u)=\left\{\frac{\sin(u/2)}{u/2}\right\}^4,
 \qquad
 g_{a,v}^{\sharp}(u)=c_{a,v}\{\psi(u)+v\psi(u-a)\},
\]
where \(a\notin2\pi\mathbb Z\), \(v>0\), \(v\ne1\), and \(c_{a,v}\) normalizes the integral.  The density is asymmetric when \(v\ne1\).  Its characteristic function has compact support because the Fourier transform of \(\psi\) is the fourfold convolution of interval indicators.  Also, the two shifted sine factors cannot vanish simultaneously; periodic compactness and comparison of \(|u|\) with \(|u-a|\) therefore give
\[
 c(1+|u|)^{-4}\le g_{a,v}^{\sharp}(u)\le C(1+|u|)^{-4}. \tag{10}
\]
Consequently it has a finite second moment.  Choose two different pairs \((a,v)\), center the resulting densities, and apply a common sufficiently small scale factor.  The resulting densities \(g_1,g_2\) remain asymmetric and nonidentical, their characteristic functions \(\varphi_1,\varphi_2\) are supported in one fixed interval \([-T_*,T_*]\), both second moments are at most \(M_e\), and the second density has mean zero.  Equation (10) remains valid with different fixed constants.

Take \(p_x=|\mathcal X|^{-1}\) and \(f_x=f^\circ\) for every \(x\).  These choices satisfy stratum positivity because \(p_{\min}<|\mathcal X|^{-1}\), the density Sobolev constraint because \(R_f>\|f^\circ\|_{H^\beta}\), compact support, and overlap because \(\kappa<\inf_I f^\circ\).  Put
\[
 m_{0,k}(a)=\frac12,
 \qquad
 m_{1,k}(a)=\frac12+\gamma\frac{h_k(a)}{f^\circ(a)},
 \qquad
 q_{j,k}=m_{j,k}f^\circ. \tag{11}
\]
Here \(\gamma>0\) is fixed smaller than the Sobolev slack \(R_q-\|f^\circ\|_{H^\beta}/2\).  Since \(J\) is contained in the interior of \(I\), \(f^\circ\) has a positive minimum on \(J\).  By (9), reducing \(\gamma\) once if necessary makes \(m_{1,k}\in[1/4,3/4]\) for every sufficiently large \(k\).  Equations (8) and (11) then give \(\|q_{j,k}\|_{H^\beta}\le R_q\).  With a uniform variable \(V\), independent of \((A,X,U_1,U_2)\), define \(Y_j(a)=\mathbf 1\{V\le m_{j,k}(a)\}\) and \(Y_j=Y_j(A)\).  This verifies consistency, boundedness because \(B_Y\ge1\), conditional unconfoundedness, and continuity of the conditional causal mean.  Thus both constructed laws belong to \(\mathcal M\).  Their ADRFs satisfy, by (9) and (11),
\[
 \|\mu_{1,k}-\mu_{0,k}\|_\infty
 =\gamma\|h_k/f^\circ\|_{L^\infty(I)}
 \ge ck^{1/2-\beta}. \tag{12}
\]

It remains to bound the observed divergence.  Let
\[
 d(s_1,s_2)=\int f^\circ(a)g_1(s_1-a)g_2(s_2-a)\,da,
 \qquad
 H_k(s_1,s_2)=\int h_k(a)g_1(s_1-a)g_2(s_2-a)\,da.
\]
Compact support of \(f^\circ\) and (10) imply
\[
 d(s_1,s_2)\ge c(1+|s_1|)^{-4}(1+|s_2|)^{-4}. \tag{13}
\]
The Fourier transform of \(H_k\) is
\[
 \widehat H_k(s,t)=\widehat h_k(s+t)\varphi_1(s)\varphi_2(t), \tag{14}
\]
and vanishes unless \((s,t)\in[-T_*,T_*]^2\).  By (6), Taylor's formula gives, for \(0\le j\le4\) and \(|u|\le2T_*\),
\[
 |\widehat h_k^{(j)}(u)|
 \le C\|h_k\|_1\frac{C_0^{2k-j}}{(2k-j)!}
 \le C\frac{C_0^{2k}}{(2k-4)!}. \tag{15}
\]
The error characteristic functions have square-integrable weak derivatives through order two because their densities have finite second moments.  Applying Plancherel to (14), also after up to two derivatives in each coordinate, and using (15), yields
\[
 \int H_k(s_1,s_2)^2(1+|s_1|)^4(1+|s_2|)^4\,ds_1\,ds_2
 \le C\frac{C_0^{4k}}{\{(2k-4)!\}^2}. \tag{16}
\]
Under the baseline law the two densities corresponding to the marks \(Y=1\) and \(Y=0\) are both \(d/2\); under the alternative their respective changes are \(\gamma H_k\) and \(-\gamma H_k\).  Therefore (13)--(16) give
\[
 \chi^2(P_{1,k,\mathrm{obs}},P_{0,k,\mathrm{obs}})
 =4\gamma^2\int\frac{H_k^2}{d}
 \le C\frac{C_0^{4k}}{\{(2k-4)!\}^2}. \tag{17}
\]
Finally, the distribution of \((X,S_1,S_2)\) is unchanged, so the probability channels and the complete unmarked observed laws coincide.  Equations (12) and (17) prove all assertions.
